senses.explanation: Very goes before an adjective or an adverb and makes it stronger: very big, very quickly. It is not used before a verb (I like it very much, not I very like it), before a comparative (much better, not very better), or before adjectives that already mean the extreme, such as huge or excellent, which take really or absolutely. Not very before an adjective is a soft way of saying the opposite: not very good means bad.

examples.text: Thank you very much for your help.

examples.note: not very: a polite way of saying bad

synonyms.note: really is more informal and can also go before a verb

compare.note: too says more than is good or wanted; very only says a lot
in American English quite is close to very; in British English it usually means fairly

senses.definition: used before an -est word such as best or biggest, or before same, own, first, last, or next, to make it stronger

examples.text: This is the very best coffee in town.
We met on the very first day of school.
Now I have a room of my very own.
She lives on the very same street as my sister.

phrases.definition: a lot; to a great degree
phrases.explanation: Very much comes after the verb and its object, or before a past participle: very much appreciated. It is the way to strengthen a verb, because very alone cannot go before a verb.

examples.text: I like the new apartment very much.
Thank you very much for coming.
Are you pleased with it? Very much so.
examples.note: very much so: a strong yes

word_family.note: the very end, at that very moment: exactly the one named, and nothing else

usage_note: Very is also an adjective meaning exactly the one named: at the very end, this very moment, the very idea! That use has a separate entry. In writing, very is often the sign of a weak word: instead of very big, a stronger adjective such as huge may read better.

learner_errors.note: Very is not used before a comparative; use much, a lot, or far.
Very cannot go before a verb; use really, or put very much after the verb: I like this song very much.
Delicious already means very good, so very adds nothing; really or absolutely can be used for emphasis.

adaptation.semantic: Very is a pure degree word. Some languages use the same word for very and for really or truly; in English, really can replace very, but very cannot replace really before a verb: I really like it.
adaptation.grammar: Very goes before adjectives and adverbs, never before verbs or comparatives: I like it very much, much better. It is not used with adjectives that already express an extreme (huge, freezing, perfect), which take really or absolutely.
adaptation.pronunciation: The first vowel is the short e of bed, and the v is made with the top teeth on the lower lip; it must not become b or w. The final y is a short ee.
